sections.h2: Your options for selling in Andover
sections.html:
Owners in Andover have three paths: hire an agent and list, sell the house yourself, or take a cash offer from a buyer who accepts the property as it stands. All three end with a signed purchase agreement and a deed recorded in Anoka County.

One duty follows you down every path. Before you sign to sell a home, Minnesota Statutes 513.55 has you hand over a written disclosure of known material facts that could significantly hurt a typical buyer's enjoyment of the house, stated in good faith. Giving it to the buyer's agent counts as giving it to the buyer.

Before you choose, pull together four items:

  • Your latest Anoka County tax statement and parcel number.
  • Permit records for plumbing, mechanical, roofing, basement or deck work done on the house.
  • The city rental license, if tenants live there.
  • A draft of the written seller disclosure.

A cash offer tends to suit owners who want a short timeline, face repairs, or hold an inherited house or tenants. Get any offer in writing, and make sure the number allows for tax owed and any open permits.

Andover is a city of about 33,874 people in Anoka County, up 3.9 percent from the 32,601 counted in 2020. It is overwhelmingly owner-occupied, and households run larger than average. Most of Andover belongs to Anoka-Hennepin School District 11, but a narrow northern strip falls under St. Francis Area Schools, District 15, so confirm the address before naming a district to a buyer.

sections.h2: Andover permits to check before you sell
sections.html:
The Building Department warns that work done without a needed permit has to be disclosed at sale and that code violations can delay or devalue a deal. Before listing, check your past projects against the permit list.

  • Permits are required for new construction, remodeling, additions and alterations, basement finishing, decks and porches, roofing, siding, irrigation systems and solid fuel fireplaces.
  • Plumbing permits cover water heaters and water softeners. Mechanical permits cover furnaces, air conditioners, boilers and gas fireplaces. Electrical work needs its own permit.
  • Septic systems need an installation permit and a designer and installer who meet Minnesota Pollution Control Agency rules. Pumping a septic tank takes a $20 permit that the pumper obtains.
  • No permit is needed for detached accessory structures under 200 square feet, sidewalks and patios, painting, flooring, cabinets, or normal maintenance such as replacing deck boards.

Homeowners may pull permits themselves, but a residential contractor is usually the better choice. Residential permits are typically approved right away or within one or two days, and about a third are applied for and paid online. The Building Department is at 1685 Crosstown Blvd NW, reachable at 763-755-8700 or building@andovermn.gov.

If a past project turns out to have no permit, ask the department what it would take to close it out before you list. Fixing that early is cheaper than a buyer's inspector finding it, and a cash buyer will still price the problem into the offer.

Single family and multifamily rentals both need a city license and inspections. A license lasts two years, each rental gets at least one inspection in that span, and a new owner cannot take over the old license.

That matters when you sell a house with tenants in it. A buyer who plans to keep renting must obtain a fresh license, so mention the tenancy early. The city's rental page links to Chapter 8 of the Andover ordinances and to the Minnesota Attorney General's landlord and tenant information.

sections.h2: Anoka County property taxes when an Andover house sells
sections.html:
Anoka County prints a single statement for each parcel, mailed in mid-March. A deed recorded after January 1 does not prompt a second mailing, so the bill goes to the earlier owner, and a duplicate must be requested. A missing statement is no excuse for a late fee.

Payments are due May 15 and October 15 with no grace period, and a deadline on a weekend rolls to Monday. Online payment goes through PayAnokaCounty, with card payments at 2.6 percent and ACH e-checks at $3.50. Checks go to Property Records and Taxation, 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, MN 55303, or to the counter at the Government Center. A free direct payment program is explained at 763-323-5400. For mailed checks the postmark decides timeliness, so ask a post office clerk for a hand-applied one.

To see what a parcel owes, search the county's property information by parcel number or by house number plus the first three characters of the street name, for example 4th rather than 4th Street. If the street shows as unassigned in the tax system, use the parcel number printed on the statement. The Government Center counter in Anoka is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, and a tax drop box sits beside it.

sections.h2: What happens from offer to closing
sections.html:
Once you accept an offer, the purchase agreement is signed and the written disclosure is already in the buyer's hands. The title company or closing agent then orders the tax figures from Anoka County, checks that no permits are left open, and prepares the deed. Closing is where the tax payoff is deducted and the deed is signed. The deed is then recorded in Anoka County, and the certificate of real estate value goes to the county auditor.

On a cash sale there is no lender appraisal or underwriting step, which is why those sales can finish quickly. The disclosure, permit and tax items do not go away, though, so start with them.

A homestead owner who sells should report it to the assessor inside 30 days, or the county can strip the homestead and add penalties. At recording, a certificate of real estate value also goes to the county auditor (Minnesota Statutes 272.115). Proposed statements for the next year land in mid-November and become final only after levies are approved in December.

A simple order keeps the closing smooth. Get the written disclosure done first. Then check permits, then the tax balance, and last any rental license. A cash buyer can often close on your schedule, but each of those items still shapes the offer, so having them ready lets you compare bids on equal terms.

faqs.q: How fast can I sell a house in Andover, MN?
faqs.a: It depends on the route. A listed sale waits on showings, financing and inspections, while a cash purchase removes the lender from the timeline. Either way, the written seller disclosure comes before your signature.

faqs.q: Is a permit required to swap a water heater in Andover?
faqs.a: Yes, a plumbing permit covers water heater and water softener replacement. A furnace or air conditioner falls under a separate mechanical permit.
Most of Andover is in Anoka-Hennepin School District 11. A small strip along the northern edge belongs to St. Francis Area Schools, District 15.

faqs.q: Who sends the Andover property tax statement?
faqs.a: Anoka County does, each March, and its Property Records and Taxation office takes payment. If nothing arrives by April 1, call 763-323-5400 for a duplicate.

faqs.q: Must I tell the county when I sell my Andover home?
faqs.a: If it was your homestead, yes: report the sale to the assessor within 30 days to avoid lost homestead status and penalties. The county auditor also receives a certificate of real estate value.
